results.name: prime_set_prime_target_effect
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all odd primes, yes rate for odd prime non-example targets minus yes rate for odd composite targets; observed > null means people pick up the "primes" concept more than the model predicts, observed < null means the model over-uses the primes rule relative to people (who treat such sets as odd numbers or ranges).
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_target_effect
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all odd primes, yes rate for odd prime non-example targets minus yes rate for odd composite targets; observed > null means people pick up the "primes" concept more than the model predicts, observed < null means the model over-uses the primes rule relative to people (who treat such sets as odd numbers or ranges).
def test_statistic(df):
    pr = np.zeros(101, dtype=bool)
    for n in range(2, 101):
        pr[n] = all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).fillna(0).astype(int).values
    has = ex > 0
    nex = has.sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    allp = (np.where(has, pr[ex] & (ex % 2 == 1), True)).all(1)
    isex = ((ex == t[:, None]) & has).any(1)
    base = (nex >= 2) & allp & ~isex & (t % 2 == 1) & (t > 1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a, b = base & pr[t], base & ~pr[t]
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: single_example_far_multiple_effect
results.description: For single-example sets with example 3-30, yes rate for targets that are multiples of the example and >=15 away minus yes rate for non-multiples >=15 away; observed > null means people extend a lone example's multiples rule to far numbers more than the model (with distance hesitance and first-example rule guess) predicts, observed < null less.
results.code:
# name: single_example_far_multiple_effect
# description: For single-example sets with example 3-30, yes rate for targets that are multiples of the example and >=15 away minus yes rate for non-multiples >=15 away; observed > null means people extend a lone example's multiples rule to far numbers more than the model (with distance hesitance and first-example rule guess) predicts, observed < null less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~sets.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(sets.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ok = single.values & (x >= 3) & (x <= 30) & (np.abs(t - x) >= 15)
    xs = np.where(x > 0, x, 1)
    mult = (t % xs) == 0
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a, b = ok & mult, ok & ~mult
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: mid_vs_far_tail_drop
results.description: Over all sets, yes rate for non-example targets 21-35 from the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 36-70 away; observed > null means generalisation drops between moderate and far distances more than the model's Gaussian-times-gamma falloff predicts, observed < null that the observed tail is flatter (a far-distance plateau the model's Gaussian kills).
results.code:
# name: mid_vs_far_tail_drop
# description: Over all sets, yes rate for non-example targets 21-35 from the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 36-70 away; observed > null means generalisation drops between moderate and far distances more than the model's Gaussian-times-gamma falloff predicts, observed < null that the observed tail is flatter (a far-distance plateau the model's Gaussian kills).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).fillna(0).astype(int).values
    has = ex > 0
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    dist = np.where(has, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 999).min(1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = (dist >= 21) & (dist <= 35)
    b = (dist >= 36) & (dist <= 70)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: within_block_late_minus_early
results.description: Within participant x set blocks of >=4 trials, yes rate on the 3rd-and-later presentations of that set minus yes rate on its first two presentations; observed != null means people's generalisation for a set drifts as they keep answering about it (observed < null: they narrow with repetition; > null: they broaden), which the model's trial-independent responses miss.
results.code:
# name: within_block_late_minus_early
# description: Within participant x set blocks of >=4 trials, yes rate on the 3rd-and-later presentations of that set minus yes rate on its first two presentations; observed != null means people's generalisation for a set drifts as they keep answering about it (observed < null: they narrow with repetition; > null: they broaden), which the model's trial-independent responses miss.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].values == 0).cumsum()
    g = pd.DataFrame({"pid": pid, "s": df["number_set"].values, "t": df["trial_index"].values, "r": df["rating"].values.astype(float)})
    g = g.sort_values(["pid", "t"])
    g["pos"] = g.groupby(["pid", "s"]).cumcount()
    g["n"] = g.groupby(["pid", "s"])["r"].transform("size")
    g = g[g["n"] >= 4]
    late = g.loc[g["pos"] >= 2, "r"]
    early = g.loc[g["pos"] < 2, "r"]
    if len(late) == 0 or len(early) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(late.mean() - early.mean())

results.name: far_shared_last_digit_yes
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share one last digit, yes rate for non-example targets with that last digit lying >=25 from the nearest example; observed > null means the model's distance hesitance over-discounts far members of a digit rule (people extend "ends in d" across the whole range), observed < null that it under-discounts them.
results.code:
# name: far_shared_last_digit_yes
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share one last digit, yes rate for non-example targets with that last digit lying >=25 from the nearest example; observed > null means the model's distance hesitance over-discounts far members of a digit rule (people extend "ends in d" across the whole range), observed < null that it under-discounts them.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).fillna(0).astype(int).values
    has = ex > 0
    nex = has.sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ld = np.where(has, ex % 10, -1)
    first = ld[:, 0]
    same = ((ld == first[:, None]) | ~has).all(1)
    dist = np.where(has, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 999).min(1)
    isex = ((ex == t[:, None]) & has).any(1)
    sel = (nex >= 2) & same & (t % 10 == first) & (dist >= 25) & ~isex
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[sel].mean())

results.name: parity_set_distance_slope
results.description: Among sets of >=3 examples all of one parity, yes rate for same-parity non-example targets >=25 from the nearest example minus that for same-parity targets <=8 away; observed > null (less negative) means people's parity generalisation is flatter over distance than the model's Gaussian hesitance implies, observed < null that it decays more steeply.
results.code:
# name: parity_set_distance_slope
# description: Among sets of >=3 examples all of one parity, yes rate for same-parity non-example targets >=25 from the nearest example minus that for same-parity targets <=8 away; observed > null (less negative) means people's parity generalisation is flatter over distance than the model's Gaussian hesitance implies, observed < null that it decays more steeply.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).fillna(0).astype(int).values
    has = ex > 0
    nex = has.sum(1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    par = np.where(has, ex % 2, -1)
    p0 = par[:, 0]
    same = ((par == p0[:, None]) | ~has).all(1)
    dist = np.where(has, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 999).min(1)
    base = (nex >= 3) & same & (t % 2 == p0) & (dist > 0)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    far, near = base & (dist >= 25), base & (dist <= 8)
    if far.sum() == 0 or near.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[far].mean() - r[near].mean())

results.name: far_rule_member_yes
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all belong to a small arithmetic rule (powers of 2-10, squares, cubes, multiples of 3-12; <=34 members), yes rate for non-example targets that are members of such a rule containing all examples and lie >=20 from the nearest example; observed > null means the model's distance hesitance over-discounts far rule members (people extend rules far), observed < null that it under-discounts them.
results.code:
# name: far_rule_member_yes
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all belong to a small arithmetic rule (powers of 2-10, squares, cubes, multiples of 3-12; <=34 members), yes rate for non-example targets that are members of such a rule containing all examples and lie >=20 from the nearest example; observed > null means the model's distance hesitance over-discounts far rule members (people extend rules far), observed < null that it under-discounts them.
def test_statistic(df):
    rules = []
    for m in range(2, 11):
        rules.append([m ** k for k in range(1, 8) if m ** k <= 100])
    rules.append([n * n for n in range(1, 11)])
    rules.append([n ** 3 for n in range(1, 5)])
    for m in range(3, 13):
        rules.append(list(range(m, 101, m)))
    M = np.zeros((len(rules), 101), dtype=bool)
    for i, r in enumerate(rules):
        M[i, r] = True
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    has = ex > 0
    nex = has.sum(1)
    # rule contains all examples: (rows, rules)
    allin = np.ones((len(df), len(rules)), dtype=bool)
    for k in range(4):
        allin &= np.where(has[:, k][:, None], M[:, ex[:, k]].T, True)
    tin = M[:, t].T
    hit = (allin & tin).any(1)
    dist = np.where(has, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 999).min(1)
    sel = (nex >= 2) & hit & (dist >= 20)
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[sel].mean())

results.name: participant_set_block_sd
results.description: For each set seen by >=2 participants with >=4 trials each (participant = run of rows starting at trial_index 0), SD across participants of their yes rate on that set, averaged over sets; observed > null means people hold a persistent personal concept guess per set (responses cluster within participant x set) that the model, which redraws independently per trial, under-produces.
results.code:
# name: participant_set_block_sd
# description: For each set seen by >=2 participants with >=4 trials each (participant = run of rows starting at trial_index 0), SD across participants of their yes rate on that set, averaged over sets; observed > null means people hold a persistent personal concept guess per set (responses cluster within participant x set) that the model, which redraws independently per trial, under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].values == 0).cumsum()
    g = pd.DataFrame({"pid": pid, "s": df["number_set"].values, "r": df["rating"].values.astype(float)})
    b = g.groupby(["s", "pid"])["r"].agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index()
    b = b[b["size"] >= 4]
    sd = b.groupby("s")["mean"].agg(["std", "size"])
    sd = sd[sd["size"] >= 2]["std"]
    return float(sd.mean()) if len(sd) else 0.0
